A Sprint session or Race may be suspended under the following conditions as outlined in Article 57 of the Sporting Regulations 2024: 

1. If Competitors or officials are placed in immediate physical danger by cars running on the track, and the Clerk of the Course deems circumstances such that the track cannot be negotiated safely, even behind the Safety Car. 

2. When the signal is given overtaking is forbidden, all cars must proceed slowly into the pit lane, with the first car to arrive proceeding directly to the pit exit. 

3. Any cars unable to return to the pit lane as a result of the track being blocked will be brought back when the track is cleared and arranged in the order they occupied before the Sprint session or race was suspended. 

4. Cars in the pit lane or pit entry at the time the Sprint session or race was suspended, as well as any cars in their garage at the time, will be arranged in the order they occupied before the Sprint session or race was suspended. 

5. All such cars will be permitted to resume the Sprint session or race when it is resumed, but must re-enter the pit lane when the Safety Car returns and may join the Sprint session or race once the last car has passed the pit exit after the re-start. 

6. The Safety Car will then be driven to the front of the line of cars in the fast lane. 

7. Whilst the Sprint session or race is suspended, the sprint session, the race nor the timekeeping system will stop. Any work performed on the cars will be restricted to what is listed in Articles 57.4b)i) to ix) and must not impede the resumption of the Sprint session or race. 

8. Only team members, officials, and duly accredited television cameramen will be permitted in the pit lane.

The survival cell, or chassis, of a Formula One car must meet stringent construction requirements to ensure the structural integrity and safety of the driver during accidents. Key points include: 

1. It must be able to withstand a compressive load of 1500 kN (157.2 tonnes). 
2. It must be made from a single piece of material, typically a composite material, which must be manufactured and tested in compliance with the FIA's Technical and Sporting Regulations. 
3. The survival cell must have sufficient rigidity and strength to protect the driver's head, neck, and chest during impact. 
4. It must be positioned such that it forms a cage around the driver, with sufficient clearance for the driver's head and limbs. 
5. The cell must not be damaged or weakened by external forces, such as fire or projectiles. 
6. It must be designed to withstand thermal loads, with a temperature rating of at least -15°C for 30 minutes. 
7. Specific areas of the cell, including the headrest, must be protected with padding and have no obstructing features to allow the padding to compress to 5% of its uncompressed thickness.
